commentary.bottom_line: One offline benchmark study suggests that tracing a subgroup performance gap to a specific bias source, here a self-reported outcome label, may account for most of that gap, but no study tested whether governance teams that systematically document bias sources produce safer or fairer tools. Seven hazard studies show that bias from labels, data composition, and historical practice exists and can shift who receives care.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a single automated benchmark using 642,205 BRFSS 2015 respondents. It attributed 89% of the sex true positive rate gap (95% CI 0.65 to 0.99) to the self-reported survey outcome. Certainty is very low because the design is offline, the result is unreplicated, and the method studied is an analytic attribution technique rather than a governance documentation process.

Hazard studies describe the failure modes this practice aims to surface. Changing the cost label shifted predicted eligibility for Black (RRR 4.31) and Asian (RRR 0.24) Medicare beneficiaries. Flipped labels cost 30.6 missed pleural effusions per 1,000 imaged patients in the targeted group. No study shows that documenting these sources caught them before they reached patients.

Most hazard studies focused on racial and ethnic minority patients, and one covered older Medicare beneficiaries. Registry-trained models recommended surgery less often for Black patients, and minority stroke patients needed higher NIHSS scores to receive thrombolysis. The single test examined a sex gap only and did not examine race, income, language, or literacy.

No study measured how long bias documentation takes, who performs it, or how consistently teams complete it in real development or purchasing workflows. The single test ran offline on survey data, so it offers no information on fidelity or burden when a governance committee applies the practice to vendor tools with limited data access.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that characterizing bias sources is necessary to assess AI bias, and the CHAI governance framework lists bias identification as a requirement. These positions rest on expert consensus. None of the supplied studies evaluates whether meeting these expectations changes device performance across subgroups.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares governance teams that use structured bias documentation, such as a Team Card or bias-source checklist, with teams using usual review. Needed studies would measure how many bias sources are found before deployment, subgroup performance after deployment, staff time required, and whether findings lead to model changes, in real health-system settings including safety-net hospitals.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test of the practice used BRFSS survey respondents and examined a sex-based gap; it did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies involved racial and ethnic minority and Medicare populations, so the evidence shows bias affects these groups but gives no indication whether bias documentation helps the underserved populations most exposed to it.
